transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-06
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Gupta (Redwood SE), Michael Turner (CTO, Kestrel), Priya Nair (Head of ML, Kestrel), Luis Martinez (SRE, Kestrel)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Customer is latency-sensitive for real-time product recommendations (p95 target ~120ms for short prompts). Interested in Dedicated for predictability but wants to validate Hosted performance first; also constraints around VPC/KMS for PII. Next: benchmark run and security doc exchange.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, really appreciate you taking the time. quick intro round robin?
[00:12] Michael Turner: Michael Turner, CTO at Kestrel. running product infra, latency is kind of our number one concern.
[00:20] Priya Nair: Priya here, head of ML. we'll be owning the model integration and evals.
[00:27] Luis Martinez: Luis, SRE. I'll be involved in network and capacity planning.
[00:32] Alex Chen: Great. Samira from Redwood is our SE she'll handle the performance/bench details. Samira?
[00:38] Samira Gupta: Hey all. quick agenda: understand your targets (p95), concurrency, streaming needs, and then talk hosting options - Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private - and propose next steps including a benchmark.
[00:48] Michael Turner: Sounds good. to be explicit, our goal is p95 generation latency under 120ms for 32-token responses at a concurrency of ~150 simultaneous requests, with spiky bursts to 500 for short periods.
[01:05] Priya Nair: Yup, and for longer responses (200-400 tokens) we care more about tokens/sec and stable tail latency \u2014 p95 around 800ms-1s is acceptable for those.
[01:15] Samira Gupta: Okay that's super helpful. couple clarifying q's: when you say 150 concurrency, is that steady-state or typical user concurrency? and what's your average tokens per second per request?
[01:26] Michael: 150 is our steady-state peak for the recommendation endpoint. typical request is 25-40 tokens, so short. bursts come from traffic surges \u2014 up to 500 concurrent for maybe 30-90 seconds.
[01:40] Luis: We also need streaming for incremental updates in the UI \u2014 low first-token latency is critical.
[01:45] Alex Chen: Good. Samira, can you talk through how Redwood handles p95 and what levers we use?
[01:50] Samira Gupta: Sure. so for Hosted we have optimized routing and continuous batching; we do prefix caching (KV cache) and kernel selection tuned per model. for Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools so your p95 is more predictable \u2014 fewer noisy neighbors. we also do adaptive batching to meet latency SLOs, but there are tradeoffs: batching helps throughput and cost but can add queuing latency unless you have reserved capacity.
[02:12] Priya: Quick Q \u2014 how does streaming impact token/sec? does streaming add extra overhead that could push us over p95?
[02:18] Samira: streaming adds a small overhead per chunk \u2014 usually a few ms \u2014 but in our measurements the large hit is from context size and model compute. for short prompts, streaming first-token latency is what you care about; we can prioritize first-token by routing to lower-batch fast-paths.
[02:33] Michael: ok. are we talking about Hosted hitting 120ms p95 for 32 tokens at 150 concurrency?
[02:38] Samira: it's feasible on Hosted with the right model and quantization level; but predictability is better on Dedicated. for Hosted, you'd see more variance during cross-region events or noisy neighbors.
[02:48] Alex: do you have any current benchmarks or a model family you're targeting?
[02:52] Priya: We currently use an open LLM (finetuned) roughly equivalent to a 34B size; it's 1.7B tokens training, and the runtime performance is similar to MPT-like architectures \u2014 we care about 8-bit quantization compatibility.
[03:07] Samira: good. our SE team can run token/sec and p95 benchmarks against a matching quantized variant. one detail: model architecture affects kernel choices, seq length, and KV cache behavior \u2014 those can change p95 a lot.
[03:21] Luis: On the infra side, if we go Dedicated we need guidance on instance types. what do you usually recommend for these sizes?
[03:27] Samira: for that model class, Dedicated on A100 80GB or H100 depending on reqs is common. we provide configs: single-GPU with optimized kernels for low-latency, or multi-GPU shards for throughput. for your steady 150 concurrency and bursts to 500, a small Dedicated pool (e.g., 4xA100 or 2xH100 with autoscale) might be needed. we'll size in the benchmark.
[03:48] Michael: cost is a factor \u2014 can you provide ballpark cost per 1M tokens in Hosted vs Dedicated?
[03:54] Alex Chen: We'll include a cost model in the pricing doc. typical pattern: Hosted simplifies ops and has variable cost; Dedicated lowers unit cost at higher commit levels but requires reserved capacity. we'll send specific numbers for your estimated qps.
[04:06] Priya: security: we need SOC2, KMS integration, and ideally on-prem or VPC for PII-sensitive inference. how does Redwood support that?
[04:15] Alex: Redwood Private offers a VPC/private deployment with customer-managed networking; we integrate with KMS/HSM and provide audit logs. we'll share SOC2 and network diagrams.
[04:24] Samira: technical note: with Private you get the same runtime features but you handle the infra. we do an onboarding to ensure kernel compatibility and we can run benchmarks in your environment.
[04:34] Luis: Are there any gotchas with prefix/KV caching and our use-case? we do a lot of near-identical prompts where caching would help.
[04:40] Samira: caching helps a lot for repeated prefixes; we have automatic prefix caching but the effectiveness depends on prompt variance. also note KV cache mis-transcriptions in logs sometimes shown as KV \"cash\" in older tools, heh.
[04:52] Michael: (laughs) noted. can you explain fallback policies if Dedicated is saturated? we want graceful degradation.
[04:58] Samira: yes, Redwood has smart routing\u2014policy-based. if Dedicated is saturated we can route to a compatible Hosted model variant (lower precision/quantized) or queue with bounded wait. for critical endpoints you can set circuit-breakers and automatic fallback to a cheaper model with shorter context to keep latency.
[05:14] Priya: For benchmarking, what metrics do you want from us? we'll provide sample prompts and a parity dataset.
[05:20] Samira: perfect \u2014 we need: representative prompts (short and long), desired p95 targets, concurrency profile (steady vs bursts), and any resourcing constraints (VPC only, no egress). we'll run both streaming and non-streaming tests and report p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and first-byte latency.
[05:36] Luis: network: our infra is behind NAT with peered VPCs; how do you handle peering and IP allowlists?
[05:42] Alex: For Private we do VPC peering or VPN; for Dedicated we also support private endpoints and IP allowlists. we'll attach network diagram examples.
[05:50] Michael: competitors \u2014 we've looked at OpenAI and Anthropic but pricing/perf tradeoffs make us consider a dedicated infra vendor. we also use Hugging Face for model hosting now.
[05:59] Samira: understood. our advantage is the production runtime controls and the cost levers (batching, quantization, cache). we'll make sure benchmarks compare apples-to-apples.
[06:08] Priya: one more on streaming \u2014 we need partial token flushing every 50ms for the UI. is that supported?
[06:14] Samira: yes, we support configurable streaming flush intervals; down to 20-50ms in many deployments. the caveat is more frequent flushes slightly increase CPU overhead on the ingress/egress path.
[06:26] Luis: how long does a typical benchmark take? we want minimal disruption to prod.
[06:30] Samira: baseline runs take a few hours; a thorough sweep (different quantization, batching configs) can be a day. we can run non-prod instances and synthetic traffic \u2014 minimal prod impact.
[06:40] Alex: let's recap next steps quickly. Samira will run the benchmark; Alex sends pricing and security docs; Luis provides concurrency logs. agreed?
[06:49] Michael: yes. Priya: yes. Luis: confirmed.
[06:53] Alex: awesome. we'll aim to have the benchmark week of 2026-04-13 and pricing to you by Friday 2026-04-09.
[06:59] Samira: I'll follow up with a benchmark checklist and sample harness repo link.
[07:05] Priya: thanks everyone.
[07:07] Michael: appreciate it.

Close notes (auto): Action items recorded above. Follow-up meeting to review benchmark results tentatively scheduled after results are ready.
